claim: RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) transcribes non-coding DNA into long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs).
source: RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) transcribes non-coding DNA into long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), but biological roles of lncRNA are unclear.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RNA Polymerase II function.

claim: Mutations in the yeast lncRNA CUT60 result in poor growth.
source: We find that mutations in the yeast lncRNA CUT60 result in poor growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Defective termination of CUT60 transcription causes read-through transcription across the ATP16 gene promoter.
source: Defective termination of CUT60 transcription causes read-through transcription across the ATP16 gene promoter.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data showing extended ATP16 transcripts in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Read-through transcription localizes chromatin signatures associated with Pol II elongation to the ATP16 promoter.
source: Read-through transcription localizes chromatin signatures associated with Pol II elongation to the ATP16 promoter.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing elevated H3K36me3/H3 levels at the ATP16 promoter in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants (Figure 4A).

claim: The act of Pol II elongation across the ATP16 promoter represses functional ATP16 expression by a Transcriptional Interference (TI) mechanism.
source: The act of Pol II elongation across this promoter represses functional ATP16 expression by a Transcriptional Interference (TI) mechanism.
evidence: Supported by ChIP data, synthetic circuit experiments, and genetic analysis with elongation factor mutants (Figure 4).

claim: Atp16p function in the mitochondrial ATP-synthase complex promotes mitochondrial DNA stability.
source: Atp16p function in the mitochondrial ATP-synthase complex promotes mitochondrial DNA stability.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006) and experimental data showing mtDNA loss in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants.

claim: ATP16 repression by TI through inefficient termination of CUT60 triggers mitochondrial genome loss.
source: ATP16 repression by TI through inefficient termination of CUT60 therefore triggers mitochondrial genome loss.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing mtDNA loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), COX3 expression analysis (Figure 1E), and growth assays on non-fermentable carbon sources (Figure 1C).

claim: The lncRNA CUT60 is divergently transcribed from the promoter of the mediator complex subunit MED2.
source: The lncRNA CUT60 is divergently transcribed from the promoter of the mediator complex subunit MED2 (Poss et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poss et al., 2013.

claim: CUT60 is located upstream in tandem of the ATP16 gene.
source: In addition, CUT60 is located upstream in tandem of the ATP16 gene encoding the δ-subunit of the mitochondrial ATP-synthase that couples proton translocation to ATP synthesis (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2003; Giraud and Velours, 1994) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by schematic representation in Figure 1A and citations.

claim: ATP16 encodes the δ-subunit of the mitochondrial ATP-synthase that couples proton translocation to ATP synthesis.
source: In addition, CUT60 is located upstream in tandem of the ATP16 gene encoding the δ-subunit of the mitochondrial ATP-synthase that couples proton translocation to ATP synthesis (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2003; Giraud and Velours, 1994) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2003 and Giraud and Velours, 1994.

claim: Native Elongating Transcript sequencing (NET-seq) data indicates higher nascent Pol II transcription of MED2 and ATP16 than of CUT60.
source: Native Elongating Transcript sequencing (NET-seq) data (Marquardt et al., 2014) indicates higher nascent Pol II transcription of the two flanking genes than of CUT60 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by NET-seq data visualization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Marquardt et al., 2014.

claim: Multiple independently generated isolates of cut60Δ::URA3 mutants had a strongly reduced growth rate compared to wild type.
source: We note that multiple independently generated isolates of cut60Δ::URA3 mutants had a strongly reduced growth rate compared to wild type (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by serial dilution growth assays shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: cut60Δ::URA3 fails to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources, indicating mitochondrial defects.
source: Strikingly, cut60Δ::URA3 fails to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources, indicating mitochondrial defects (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by growth assays on glycerol and ethanol shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Diploids resulting from crosses of cut60Δ::URA3 with mip1Δ fail to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources.
source: We find that diploids resulting from crosses of cut60Δ::URA3 with mip1Δ fail to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources, while they show growth on the fermentable carbon source glucose (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by test cross data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mitochondrial DNA level in cut60Δ::URA3 is reduced compared to wild type yeast.
source: We find that the mitochondrial DNA level in cut60Δ::URA3 and mipΔ1 controls are reduced compared to wild type yeast.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: No qPCR signal corresponding to mtDNA is detected in cut60Δ::URA3, suggesting a ρ0 phenotype.
source: We detect no qPCR signal corresponding to mtDNA, suggesting a ρ0 phenotype in cut60Δ::URA3.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: COX3 expression cannot be detected in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants.
source: While we can detect strong COX3 expression in wild type, we fail to detect any COX3 expression in the p0 control mutant mip1Δ and cut60Δ::URA3.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression of the downstream ATP16 is strongly reduced in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants.
source: Expression of the downstream ATP16 is strongly reduced in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants, while we detect no expression changes of the MED2 gene (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No expression changes of the MED2 gene are detected in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants.
source: Expression of the downstream ATP16 is strongly reduced in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants, while we detect no expression changes of the MED2 gene (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An extended ATP16 transcript is observed in rrp6Δ and at higher levels in xrn1Δ backgrounds in cut60Δ::URA3 mutants.
source: We noticed a different size profile of ATP16 RNA in cut60Δ::URA3 mutant strains with RNA degradation defects through rrp6Δ or xrn1Δ (Figure 2A). While we detect no ATP16 mRNA expression of the expected size in the mutants, we observe an extended ATP16 transcript in rrp6Δ, and at higher levels in xrn1Δ.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The extended ATP16 transcript detected in the cut60Δ::URA3 mutant represents 5'-extension that originates from the CUT60 promoter.
source: Both probes detect a transcript coinciding in size with the extended ATP16 transcript. This data suggest that the extended ATP16 transcript detected in the cut60Δ::URA3 mutant represents 5'-extension that originates from the CUT60 promoter and fails to efficiently terminate, resulting in read-through transcription into ATP16.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data using URA3 and ATP16 promoter probes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A similar repression of ATP16 is observed in mutants replacing CUT60 with SUT129.
source: A similar repression of ATP16 is observed in mutants replacing CUT60 with SUT129 (cut60Δ::SUT129), indicating that this effect is not dependent on the URA3 sequence (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expressing CUT60 in trans from the SUT129 regulatory regions does not restore ATP16 expression.
source: However, expressing CUT60 in trans from the SUT129 regulatory regions (sut129Δ::CUT60) does not restore ATP16 expression (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CUT60 has a cis-acting function to promote ATP16 expression.
source: These data indicate a cis-acting function of the CUT60 locus to promote ATP16 expression, either as DNA element or non-coding transcript.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trans expression does not restore ATP16 expression.

claim: All complementation constructs (V1-V4) restore ATP16 expression to wild-type level.
source: Our results indicate that all constructs restore ATP16 expression to the level detected in wild type.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data and quantification shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: There is no significantly different ATP16 expression between construct V1 (lacking CUT60) and construct V2 (including CUT60).
source: Our statistical tests show no significantly different ATP16 expression between these constructs.
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DNA sequence elements located within the CUT60 sequence do not provide promoter function to explain reduced ATP16 expression in cells lacking CUT60 sequences.
source: These data strongly argue against DNA sequence elements providing promoter function located in CUT60 as explanation for reduced ATP16 expression and growth in cells lacking CUT60 sequences.
evidence: Inferred from the complementation data showing V1 (lacking CUT60) restores ATP16 expression.

claim: SUT129 cannot substitute CUT60 function.
source: In cut60Δ::SUT129, an extended ATP16 transcript with reduced expression is detected (Figure 3A). We conclude that SUT129 cannot substitute CUT60 function.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATP16 expression is restored when the 5'-SUT129-3'-CUT60 hybrid replaces CUT60.
source: Strikingly, ATP16 expression is restored when the 5'-SUT129-3'-CUT60 hybrid replaces CUT60 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Efficient transcriptional termination is mapped to the 3'-half of CUT60.
source: The detection of a SUT-like transcript resulting from the 5'-SUT129-3'-CUT60 hybrid maps efficient transcriptional termination to the 3'-half of CUT60.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the 5'-SUT129-3'-CUT60 hybrid restores ATP16 expression while 5'-CUT60-3'-SUT129 does not.

claim: Efficient transcriptional termination of CUT60 promotes ATP16 expression.
source: These data suggest that efficient transcriptional termination of CUT60 promotes ATP16 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the hybrid construct experiments.

claim: The essential Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) pathway mediates termination of Pol II transcription of short non-coding transcripts including CUTs and SUTs.
source: The essential budding yeast Nrd1-Nab3-Sen1 (NNS) pathway mediates termination of Pol II transcription of short non-coding transcripts including CUTs and SUTs (Porrua and Libri, 2015; Schulz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Porrua and Libri, 2015 and Schulz et al., 2013.

claim: Hypomorphic nrd1 mutations reveal 3'-extended CUT60 RNA species.
source: A role for NNS-mediated transcriptional termination of CUT60 is supported by hypomorphic nrd1 mutations that reveal 3'-extended CUT60 RNA species (Marquardt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marquardt et al., 2011.

claim: Conditional Nrd1 depletion results in more Pol II-associated RNA downstream of CUT60.
source: Nascent transcription data (Pol II PAR-CLIP) following conditional Nrd1 depletion support a direct role of Nrd1 in CUT60 termination as depletion results in more Pol II-associated RNA downstream of CUT60 (Schaughency et al., 2014) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schaughency et al., 2014 and visualization in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: nrd1-1 and nrd1Δ151-214 mutants fail to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources.
source: Strikingly, nrd1-1, nrd1Δ151–214 and the mip1Δ ρ0 control fail to grow on non-fermentable carbon sources, while we can recapitulate the reduced growth phenotype of both mutant alleles on fermentable carbon sources.
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both nrd1 mutant alleles reduce ATP16 expression by about 40% compared to their respective isogenic controls.
source: Both nrd1 mutant alleles reduce ATP16 expression by about 40% compared to their respective isogenic controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by northern blot quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CUT60 termination by the NNS pathway promotes ATP16 expression and mtDNA maintenance.
source: In conclusion, these data suggest that CUT60 termination by the NNS pathway promotes ATP16 expression and mtDNA maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from the nrd1 mutant phenotypes.

claim: ATP16 expression increased compared to cut60Δ::URA3 controls in the cut60Δ::CUT217, cut60Δ::CUT170 and cut60Δ::#78 replacements.
source: ATP16 expression increased compared to cut60Δ::URA3 controls in the cut60Δ::CUT217, cut60Δ::CUT170 and cut60Δ::#78 even though not fully to wild type level (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The cut60Δ::CUT95, cut60Δ::CUT277 and cut60Δ::CUT48 replacements result in no detectable ATP16 expression increase.
source: However, the cut60Δ::CUT95, cut60Δ::CUT277 and cut60Δ::CUT48 replacements result in no detectable ATP16 expression increase (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reintroducing CUT60 restores ATP16 expression, arguing against epigenetic effects preventing ATP16 expression in CUT replacement strains.
source: Reintroducing CUT60 restores ATP16 expression, arguing against epigenetic effects preventing ATP16 expression in CUT replacement strains (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ATP16 expression increases with all three strategies to enhance termination of URA3 transcription.
source: Strikingly, ATP16 expression increases with all three strategies to enhance termination of URA3 transcription.
evidence: Supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The process of transcriptional termination promotes ATP16 expression.
source: These results strongly argue for a model in which the process of transcriptional termination promotes ATP16 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the terminator addition experiments.

claim: H3K36me3/H3 levels are significantly increased in cut60Δ::URA3 compared to controls in the ATP16 promoter region.
source: However, H3K36me3/H3 levels are significantly increased in cut60Δ::URA3 compared to controls in the ATP16 promoter region (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ATP16 repression is associated with elevated chromatin signatures of Pol II elongation at the ATP16 promoter.
source: Our ChIP analyses indicate that ATP16 repression is associated with elevated chromatin signatures of Pol II elongation at the ATP16 promoter.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP data showing elevated H3K36me3 at the ATP16 promoter.

claim: YFP expression from the ATP16 promoter in circuit II is significantly reduced compared to circuit I.
source: YFP expression from the ATP16 promoter in circuit II is significantly reduced compared to circuit I, while mCherry expression appears largely unaffected (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: YFP fluorescence is normally distributed across thousands of individual cells, supporting the hypothesis that ATP16 expression is gradually reduced in a homogenous population.
source: YFP fluorescence is normally distributed across thousands of individual cells, supporting the hypothesis that ATP16 expression is gradually reduced in a homogenous population (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by histogram data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: set2Δ mutation increases YFP expression in circuit II but not in circuit I.
source: While mCherry expression is unchanged in set2Δ mutants, YFP expression increases (Figure 4D). This effect of set2Δ is not observed in circuit I (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: spt16-197 and spt6-1004 mutants increase YFP expression specifically in circuit II.
source: Both mutants increase YFP expression specifically in circuit II, consistent with TI suppression (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Pol II elongation factors previously associated with gene repression by TI are required for full repression of the ATP16 promoter region when the termination of upstream lncRNA transcription is inefficient.
source: These data show that Pol II elongation factors previously associated with gene repression by TI are required for full repression of the ATP16 promoter region when the termination of upstream lncRNA transcription is inefficient.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic analysis with Set2, Spt6, and Spt16 mutants.

claim: Efficient termination of upstream lncRNA transcription ensures ATP16 promoter activity.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that efficient termination of upstream lncRNA transcription ensures ATP16 promoter activity.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental data.

claim: CUT60 termination promotes functional ATP16 expression, the maintenance of mitochondrial DNA and yeast growth.
source: CUT60 termination promotes functional ATP16 expression, the maintenance of mitochondrial DNA and yeast growth.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental data.

claim: The dependence of mitochondrial DNA stability on CUT60 termination provides a compelling example for the biological significance of pervasive non-coding transcription in genomes.
source: All in all, the dependence of mitochondrial DNA stability on CUT60 termination provides a compelling example for the biological significance of pervasive non-coding transcription in genomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: ncDNA sequences vastly outnumber protein coding DNA sequences in most eukaryotic genomes.
source: ncDNA sequences vastly outnumber protein coding DNA sequences in most eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Genome-wide Pol II activity at ncDNA is referred to as 'pervasive transcription' of eukaryotic genomes.
source: Genome-wide Pol II activity at ncDNA is referred to as 'pervasive transcription' of eukaryotic genomes (Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jensen et al., 2013.

claim: The expression levels of lncRNA are generally lower than those of genes.
source: Indeed, the expression levels of lncRNA are generally lower than those of genes (Schlackow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schlackow et al., 2017.

claim: Reasons for low expression levels of lncRNA include a combination of tissue-specific expression and targeted lncRNA degradation.
source: Reasons for low expression levels of lncRNA include a combination of tissue-specific expression and targeted lncRNA degradation (Deveson et al., 2017; Jensen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deveson et al., 2017 and Jensen et al., 2013.

claim: lncRNA transcription can be strong, for example divergent lncRNA transcription from gene promoters.
source: Measurements of nascent Pol II transcription reveal that lncRNA transcription can be strong, for example divergent lncRNA transcription from gene promoters (Churchman and Weissman, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Churchman and Weissman, 2011.

claim: The strength of divergent lncRNA transcription is actively regulated at the level of initiation through chromatin-based mechanisms.
source: The strength of divergent lncRNA transcription is actively regulated at the level of initiation through chromatin-based mechanisms (Marquardt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marquardt et al., 2014.

claim: As a class, lncRNA molecules are poorly conserved on sequence level.
source: As a class, lncRNA molecules are poorly conserved on sequence level, which challenges the idea of an evolutionarily conserved function of lncRNA (Graur et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graur et al., 2015.

claim: Cryptic Unstable Transcripts (CUTs) accumulate in mutants of the nuclear exosome 3'-to-5' RNA decay pathway.
source: Cryptic Unstable Transcripts (CUTs) accumulate in mutants of the nuclear exosome 3'-to-5' RNA decay pathway (Davis and Ares, 2006; Wyers et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis and Ares, 2006; Wyers et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations in the 5'-to-3' cytoplasmic decapping-based RNA degradation pathway define Xrn1-sensitive Unstable Transcripts (XUTs).
source: Mutations in the 5'-to-3' cytoplasmic decapping-based RNA degradation pathway define Xrn1-sensitive Unstable Transcripts (XUTs) (van Dijk et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Dijk et al., 2011.

claim: SUTs are targeted for degradation by both the nuclear exosome and the cytoplasmic Xrn1 pathway.
source: SUTs are targeted for degradation by both the nuclear exosome and the cytoplasmic Xrn1 pathway (Marquardt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marquardt et al., 2011.

claim: A combination of three molecular hallmarks associated with early stages of Pol II transcription recruit NNS to nascent lncRNA transcripts: Histone 3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), RNA consensus motifs in nascent lncRNA, and phosphorylation of the serine five residue in the Pol II largest subunit C-terminal repeat domain (Pol II CTD).
source: A combination of three molecular hallmarks associated with early stages of Pol II transcription recruit NNS to nascent lncRNA transcripts: Histone 3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3), RNA consensus motifs in nascent lncRNA, and phosphorylation of the serine five residue in the Pol II largest subunit C-terminal repeat domain (Pol II CTD) (Carroll et al., 2007; Terzi et al., 2011; Vasiljeva et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carroll et al., 2007; Terzi et al., 2011; Vasiljeva et al., 2008.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at tyrosine 1 decreases NNS recruitment.
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at tyrosine 1 has the opposite effect and decreases NNS recruitment (Yurko et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yurko et al., 2017.

claim: NNS-mediated transcriptional termination of CUTs is directly linked to the recruitment of the nuclear exosome RNA degradation machinery.
source: NNS-mediated transcriptional termination of CUTs is directly linked to the recruitment of the nuclear exosome RNA degradation machinery (Vasiljeva and Buratowski, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vasiljeva and Buratowski, 2006.

claim: Equivalent pathways ensure that early transcription termination of lncRNA is linked to co-transcriptional degradation by the nuclear exosome in mammals.
source: While NNS components are specific to budding yeast, equivalent pathways ensure that early transcription termination of lncRNA is linked to co-transcriptional degradation by the nuclear exosome in mammals (Ntini et al., 2013; Ogami et al., 2017; Preker et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ntini et al., 2013; Ogami et al., 2017; Preker et al., 2008.

claim: The termination of Pol II transcription for polyadenylated RNAs is currently best described by the 'Torpedo Model'.
source: The termination of Pol II transcription for polyadenylated RNAs is currently best described by the 'Torpedo Model' (Kim et al., 2004; Richard and Manley, 2009; West et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2004; Richard and Manley, 2009; West et al., 2004.

claim: Failures in the Pol II termination process can impact on genomic stability.
source: Failures in the Pol II termination process can impact on genomic stability (Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012.

claim: Inefficient termination can blur the boundaries of neighboring transcription units with negative effects on gene expression.
source: Inefficient termination can blur the boundaries of neighboring transcription units with negative effects on gene expression (Ard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ard et al., 2017.

claim: TI of gene promoters by read-through transcription of upstream protein coding genes has been detected in additional organisms.
source: TI of gene promoters by read-through transcription of upstream protein coding genes has since been detected in additional organisms (Greger et al., 2000; Hedtke and Grimm, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greger et al., 2000; Hedtke and Grimm, 2009.

claim: TI repression of gene promoters can be triggered by overlapping lncRNA transcription.
source: TI repression of gene promoters can also be triggered by overlapping lncRNA transcription (Ard et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016; Mellor et al., 2016; Touat-Todeschini et al., 2017), or by termination failures of transcripts embedded within lncRNA such as pri-miRNA (Dhir et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ard et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016; Mellor et al., 2016; Touat-Todeschini et al., 2017; Dhir et al., 2015.

claim: Upstream lncRNA transcription across the downstream gene promoter represents a mechanism to adjust gene expression to the environmental conditions in budding yeast.
source: Upstream lncRNA transcription across the downstream gene promoter represents a mechanism to adjust gene expression to the environmental conditions in budding yeast (Martens et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martens et al., 2004.

claim: No initiation from the SER3 promoter occurs through co-transcriptional changes in the chromatin structure associated with Pol II elongation when Pol II is actively transcribing across the promoter.
source: Even though Pol II is actively transcribing across the promoter of the downstream SER3 gene required for serine biosynthesis, no initiation from the SER3 promoter occurs through co-transcriptional changes in the chromatin structure associated with Pol II elongation (Hainer et al., 2011; Martens et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hainer et al., 2011; Martens et al., 2004.

claim: Gene expression can be attenuated by depositing methylation marks over promoters by cryptic transcription.
source: Similarly, gene expression can be attenuated by depositing methylation marks over promoters by cryptic transcription (Kim et al., 2012; Pinskaya et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2012; Pinskaya et al., 2009.

claim: In atp16 mutant backgrounds the loss of the mitochondrial genome represents a survival strategy.
source: Interestingly, in atp16 mutant backgrounds the loss of the mitochondrial genome represents a survival strategy (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006.

claim: Loss of the mitochondrial genome efficiently blocks proton leakage, as the two subunits encoding the core of the ATP-synthase proton channel (ATP6 and ATP9) are located on the mitochondrial genome.
source: However, acquiring ρ0 efficiently blocks proton leakage, as the two subunits encoding the core of the ATP-synthase proton channel (ATP6 and ATP9) are located on the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of ATP6 and ATP9 genes.

claim: Loss of mtDNA disrupts proton channel formation to prevent uncoupling of the ATP synthase in the absence of a functional δ-subunit.
source: Hence, loss of the mitochondrial genome disrupts proton channel formation to prevent uncoupling of the ATP synthase in the absence of a functional δ-subunit (Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duvezin-Caubet et al., 2006.

claim: Divergent transcription of lncRNA from eukaryotic gene promoters represents an important source of lncRNA.
source: Divergent transcription of lncRNA from eukaryotic gene promoters represents an important source of lncRNA (Sigova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sigova et al., 2013.

claim: Divergent lncRNA transcription is repressed by lncRNA degradation.
source: Divergent lncRNA transcription is repressed by lncRNA degradation (Almada et al., 2013; Ntini et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009), and by a repressive chromatin architecture (Jin et al., 2017; Marquardt et al., 2014; Rege et al., 2015; Tan-Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Almada et al., 2013; Ntini et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2017; Marquardt et al., 2014; Rege et al., 2015; Tan-Wong et al., 2012.

claim: Inefficient transcriptional termination and environmentally regulated expression define the species of budding yeast SUTs.
source: Inefficient transcriptional termination and environmentally regulated expression define the species of budding yeast SUTs (Marquardt et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marquardt et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Regulation of FLO11 expression is regulated at the level of individual cells resulting in heterogeneous expression states.
source: While regulation of FLO11 expression is regulated at the level of individual cells resulting in heterogeneous expression states (Bumgarner et al., 2012), our analysis of circuit II suggests that ATP16 expression is reduced in a homogenous population.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bumgarner et al., 2012.

claim: Many human lncRNA share characteristic cell-type-specific and environmentally regulated expression.
source: While the SUT nomenclature is specific to budding yeast, it should be noted that many human lncRNA share characteristic cell-type-specific and environmentally regulated expression (Deveson et al., 2017) and cis-acting functions are increasingly appreciated (Engreitz et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deveson et al., 2017 and Engreitz et al., 2016.

claim: Divergent lncRNA transcription of human promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTs) may overlap with downstream genes reminiscent of the MED2-CUT60-ATP16 circuitry.
source: Divergent lncRNA transcription of human promoter upstream transcripts (PROMPTs) may overlap with downstream genes reminiscent of the MED2-CUT60-ATP16 circuitry (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Strong binding of Nrd1 and Nab3 to CUT60 is detected by PAR-CLIP, suggesting CUT60 represents a strong transcriptional terminator for the NNS pathway.
source: We detect strong binding of Nrd1 and Nab3 to CUT60 by PAR-CLIP, suggesting CUT60 represents a strong transcriptional terminator for the NNS pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by PAR-CLIP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ATP16 promoter shows little evidence of divergent lncRNA transcription.
source: Even though most promoters in eukaryotic genomes initiate transcription bi-directionally (Preker et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2008), the ATP16 promoter shows little evidence of divergent lncRNA transcription (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by NET-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, and citations to Preker et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2008.

claim: Divergent lncRNA transcription could provide an opposing wave of Pol II transcription that may trigger termination of incoming read-through transcripts by polymerase collisions.
source: Divergent lncRNA transcription could conceivably provide an opposing wave of Pol II transcription that may trigger termination of incoming read-through transcripts by polymerase collisions, as proposed for the yeast BAT2 promoter (Hobson et al., 2012; Mellor et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hobson et al., 2012; Mellor et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2014.

claim: The ATP16 promoter lacks binding sites for the Reb1p and Rap1p transcription factors that prevent read-through transcription by a road-blocking mechanism.
source: The ATP16 promoter lacks binding sites for the Reb1p and Rap1p transcription factors that prevent read-through transcription by a road-blocking mechanism, which may also contribute to the sensitivity for read-through repression (Candelli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Candelli et al., 2018.

claim: Promoter repression by TI can be partially overcome by increasing the levels of promoter-specific transcription factors to trigger transcriptional initiation.
source: It has previously been established that promoter repression by TI can be partially overcome by increasing the levels of promoter-specific transcription factors to trigger transcriptional initiation (Greger et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greger et al., 2000.

claim: Set2p is required for TI by sufficiently long upstream interfering transcripts.
source: Set2p is required for TI by sufficiently long upstream interfering transcripts (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2016.

claim: The histone chaperones Spt6p and Spt16p are required for TI without an apparent size limit of the interfering transcript.
